content.summary: Welcome to the reading mission on airport travel dilemmas. In this lesson, you will read about common travel challenges such as missed connecting flights, lost baggage, and overbooked planes. You will learn how to understand formal announcements, complaints, and information notices at busy transit hubs.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Perfect for recent events, Modal Verbs for formal requests, and Passive Voice for situations where the agent is unknown or less important.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key terms related to flights, baggage, transit visas, and passenger compensation claims.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for specific details like flight numbers, gate changes, and compensation rules, alongside skimming for general understanding of travel problem descriptions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about airport travel dilemmas.
Locate specific details such as gate numbers, baggage claim locations, and flight status updates.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns involving the Present Perfect and Passive Voice in transit contexts.

contextWarmup.prompt: What should you do first if your checked luggage does not appear at the baggage claim carousel?
options: Go directly to the airline service desk or baggage service office to file a report.
Leave the airport immediately and wait for the airline to call your mobile phone.
Board another flight to your home country without telling airport security.
contextWarmup.explanation: When luggage is missing, you must report it at the airline baggage service desk before leaving the secure customs area to obtain a Property Irregularity Report.

rules: Use the Present Perfect to explain recent problems that affect your current situation: 'My luggage has been lost' or 'The flight has been delayed for three hours'.

Use Modal Verbs for polite and formal inquiries at the service desk: 'Could you please check my booking?', 'Would it be possible to reroute my flight?', or 'I would like to file a complaint about...' .

Use Passive Voice to focus on the problem rather than the person who caused it: 'I was informed that my flight was cancelled', 'My booking was updated', or 'Passengers are being transferred to a hotel'.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Active and Passive Voice in Service Complaints
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often try to use active sentences when they do not know who caused the flight problem, which leads to unnatural phrasing.
commonTrap.wrong: Somebody lost my baggage and somebody cancelled my flight without any reason.
commonTrap.correct: My baggage was lost and my flight was cancelled unexpectedly.

paragraphs: Travelers arriving at Terminal 3 experienced a stressful morning after heavy fog caused severe disruptions across international departures. Flight QR402 to London was delayed by more than four hours, leaving hundreds of passengers waiting in the departure lounge. Many individuals worried about missing their connecting flight in Doha, which made the atmosphere tense near the information counters.

At the customer service desk, Sarah Jenkins stood patiently with her boarding pass in hand. Her flight had been overbooked, and airline representatives informed her that she needed to be rerouted through another city. 'Could you please check if there is an alternative flight this afternoon?' she asked politely. The agent quickly reviewed her file, issued a meal voucher, and confirmed a seat on an evening departure.

Meanwhile, in the baggage claim area, Mark discovered that his suitcase had not arrived on carousel number 4. After checking with the baggage service office, he learned his bag was left behind at the departure airport due to loading delays. He filled out a missing luggage report and was assured that his belongings would be delivered directly to his hotel the next morning.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Travel Dilemmas, Booking Flights & Problem Resolution at Transit Hubs

content.summary: Master the art of writing professional transit complaints, flight inquiry messages, and problem-resolution emails using the Present Perfect, modal verbs, and the passive voice at B1 level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Perfect for Recent Transit Issues
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + has/have + past participle + time marker
blueprintItems.example: My flight has been delayed for three hours at Gate 12.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Polite Modal Verbs for Formal Requests
blueprintItems.formula: Modal (Could / Would) + subject + please + base verb + object
blueprintItems.example: Could you please check my luggage status in the system?

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Passive Voice for Objective Problem Reporting
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + auxiliary (was/were/is) + past participle + by agent
blueprintItems.example: My original booking was cancelled without prior notice.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize airport codes, airlines, and proper names.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I flew from JFK Airport to Heathrow with British Airways.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i flew from jfk airport to heathrow with british airways.
mechanicsRules.why: Specific locations and company names are proper nouns.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use formal closing phrases in complaint and inquiry emails.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I look forward to your prompt response. Sincerely, John Doe
mechanicsRules.why: Formal writing at transit hubs requires professional and polite sign-offs.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place commas correctly after introductory time or prepositional phrases.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Due to heavy fog, the flight was postponed.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Due to heavy fog the flight was postponed.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma clarifies the transition from the introductory phrase to the main clause.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Polite requests in customer service scenarios utilize modals like 'Could you please' or 'Would you please'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this affirmative sentence into a negative sentence using the Present Perfect:

practicumQuestions.instruction: Convert the following active sentence into the passive voice:

targetAnswers: All departures have been delayed due to the storm.

practicumQuestions.explanation: With plural subjects in the Present Perfect passive, use 'have been' plus the past participle.

practicumQuestions.explanation: Sentences must begin with a capital letter, days of the week must be capitalized, and introductory clauses often take a comma.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'so' to show the consequence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: The transit desk was closed. We had to wait at the gate.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'so' to connect the cause and effect.
targetAnswers: The transit desk was closed, so we had to wait at the gate.
The transit desk was closed so we had to wait at the gate.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The conjunction 'so' introduces a clause expressing the result or consequence of the preceding clause.

pillars.name: Polite Request Intonation

pillars.name: Thought Group Chunking

pillars.explanation: Break long sentences about flight numbers and gate changes into digestible chunks so agents understand your situation instantly.
